What Rezpeg Actually Does 
 
Core Biology of Tregs and FOXP3 
FOXP3 (forkhead box P3) is the master transcription factor that defines the Treg lineage and maintains their suppressive identity. 
When FOXP3 is expressed at high levels, it: 
 
Directly and indirectly turns on a set of genes that make the cell a functional Treg (including IL2RA, which encodes CD25). 
Turns off genes that would make the cell behave like a conventional effector T cell (e.g., it represses IL-2 production by the Treg itself). 
Stabilizes the Treg phenotype so the cell stays regulatory rather than converting into an effector cell. 
 
There is a positive feedback loop that is central to your question: 
 
IL-2 signaling (mainly through the JAK–STAT5 pathway) causes phosphorylated STAT5 to bind to the FOXP3 locus and promote FOXP3 transcription. 
FOXP3 then binds to the IL2RA (CD25) promoter and increases CD25 expression. 
Higher CD25 makes the high-affinity IL-2 receptor (IL-2Rαβγ), so the Treg becomes even more sensitive to the low levels of IL-2 that are normally present in the body. 
This further reinforces STAT5 signaling → more FOXP3 → more CD25, creating a self-reinforcing loop. 
 
Tregs constitutively express high levels of CD25, which is why they can respond to very low concentrations of IL-2 that conventional T cells (which mainly use the intermediate-affinity βγ receptor) ignore. 
Rezpegaldesleukin is a pegylated recombinant IL-2 designed so that: 
 
The PEG chains lower its overall affinity and slow its association rate. 
It preferentially engages the intermediate-affinity IL-2 receptor (βγ chains, often referred to loosely as the “gamma” pathway) in a way that strongly favors Tregs over effector T cells and NK cells. 
Because Tregs already express high CD25, they form the high-affinity trimer more readily and receive a stronger, more sustained signal. 
 
The result is selective expansion and activation of Tregs (especially the CD25bright subset) without meaningful expansion of conventional CD4/CD8 T cells. 
How This “Resets” or Ramps Up the Treg Set Point 
In inflammatory diseases such as atopic dermatitis or alopecia areata, the Treg pool is often numerically reduced or functionally impaired. Short courses of rezpeg do several things: 
 
They drive a rapid, dose-dependent increase in total Tregs and especially CD25bright Tregs (in the Phase 1b AD study, peak increases of ~4–10-fold in CD25bright Tregs were seen after the first 1–2 doses). 
The boosted IL-2/STAT5 signal increases FOXP3 expression and locks in higher CD25 expression. 
The expanded Tregs become more suppressive (higher expression of other regulatory molecules) and can better control effector responses (Th1, Th2, Th17 pathways). 
Because of the FOXP3–CD25 positive feedback loop, many of these cells maintain elevated CD25 and FOXP3 even after the drug is stopped. This is why, in the Phase 1b AD study (only 12 weeks of induction), clinical responses and elevated CD25bright Tregs persisted for many months off-drug in a substantial fraction of responders. 
 
In short: rezpeg does not just temporarily expand the existing Treg pool. It strengthens the internal positive-feedback circuit (IL-2 → STAT5 → FOXP3 → CD25 → more IL-2 sensitivity), so the cells themselves raise their own “set point” for survival, proliferation, and suppressive function. Once that new higher baseline is established, the Tregs can continue producing/maintaining the regulatory environment with only the low levels of endogenous IL-2 that are normally present. 
That is the mechanistic basis for the hope of a remittive (rather than purely continuous-suppressive) effect that was first seen with the short 12-week induction in the Phase 1b AD trials and is being further tested in the longer Phase 2b programs.
